exercises.name: Lying Lateral Neck Flexion (Side Neck Raise)

muscles.name: Abdominals (Rectus Abdominis & Obliques)

landmarks.notes: Abs respond to progressive overload like any muscle; add resistance rather than only doing endless bodyweight reps. Estimate only.

muscles.training_notes: Load spinal flexion (weighted crunches, cable crunches, hanging raises) and train the obliques with rotation (cable wood-chops) and anti-rotation (Pallof press, side planks). Progressive resistance beats high-rep-only work.

muscles.name: Biceps Brachii (& Brachialis)

landmarks.notes: Receives meaningful indirect work from all pulling; count some pulling volume as fractional biceps volume. Estimate only.

muscles.frequency_notes: ~2x/week direct, on top of back-day involvement.
muscles.training_notes: Train the long head at length (incline or overhead-elbow curls) and include a supinated curl. Brachialis benefits from hammer/neutral-grip work.

muscles.name: Calves (Gastrocnemius & Soleus)

landmarks.notes: Little indirect work; tolerates frequent training. Knee angle selects the head trained. Estimate only.

muscles.frequency_notes: Responds to high frequency (2-4x/week) of direct work.
muscles.training_notes: Straight-leg raises (standing/leg-press) target the gastrocnemius; bent-knee (seated) raises target the soleus. Pause in the stretched bottom position; avoid bouncing.

muscles.name: Chest (Pectoralis Major)

landmarks.notes: Model-based estimate of weekly hard sets, not a measured constant. Individualize from your own response. Includes only direct/near-direct chest work; heavy pressing already loads the chest.

muscles.frequency_notes: Train ~2x/week to distribute volume across incline and flat pressing plus a fly variation.
muscles.training_notes: Cover both heads: incline work biases the clavicular head, flat/decline the sternal head. Include a lengthened-position movement (deep dumbbell press or fly).

muscles.name: Forearms (Wrist Flexors & Extensors)

landmarks.notes: Grip and forearm flexors get heavy indirect work from pulling and carrying. Add direct work if lagging. Estimate only.

muscles.training_notes: Wrist curls/extensions and loaded carries or heavy holds. Brachioradialis is trained by hammer/reverse curls.

muscles.name: Anterior Deltoid (Front Delt)

landmarks.notes: Heavily worked by all horizontal and overhead pressing, so direct volume needs are modest for most people. Estimate only.

muscles.frequency_notes: Usually covered by pressing frequency; add little dedicated work unless prioritized.
muscles.training_notes: Overhead and incline pressing provide most of the stimulus. Front raises are rarely needed.

muscles.name: Glutes (Gluteus Maximus, Medius, Minimus)

landmarks.notes: Heavily worked by squats, hinges, and lunges, so direct MEV is low for most people. Estimate only.

muscles.frequency_notes: ~2x/week; largely covered by compound lower-body training.
muscles.training_notes: Squats and deadlifts load the glutes at long lengths (deep hip flexion); hip thrusts add short-position, high-tension work. Add abduction work for the medius/minimus if targeting shape.

muscles.name: Hamstrings

landmarks.notes: Two functions (knee flexion and hip extension) usually need separate exercises. High-eccentric work (RDLs) causes notable damage; individualize volume. Estimate only.

muscles.frequency_notes: ~2x/week; separate a hip-hinge day from a knee-flexion (leg curl) day if volume is high.
muscles.training_notes: Train BOTH functions: Romanian deadlifts (hip extension, loaded stretch) and leg curls (knee flexion). Seated leg curls load the lengthened position more than lying/standing, and grow the hamstrings more (Maeo 2021: +14% vs +9% muscle volume, seated vs prone).

muscles.name: Latissimus Dorsi

landmarks.notes: Back musculature generally tolerates relatively high weekly volume. Estimate only; individualize.

muscles.frequency_notes: ~2x/week, split across vertical (pulldown/pull-up) and horizontal (row) pulling.
muscles.training_notes: Use both a vertical and a horizontal pull. Emphasize the stretched position (full reach overhead on pulldowns/pull-ups).

muscles.name: Neck (Sternocleidomastoid & Cervical Extensors)

landmarks.notes: Direct neck training is niche; use very light loads, slow tempo, and pain-free ranges. Volume needs are low. Estimate only.

muscles.frequency_notes: Tolerates 2-3x/week of low-load direct work if trained at all.
muscles.recovery_notes: Cervical spine is sensitive — introduce gradually and never train into pain.
muscles.training_notes: Train flexion and extension (and optionally lateral flexion) with a harness or plate. Optional for most lifters; relevant for contact-sport athletes.

muscles.name: Quadriceps

landmarks.notes: High per-set systemic fatigue on squats limits recoverable volume relative to smaller muscles. Estimate only.

muscles.frequency_notes: ~2x/week; balance heavy squats against higher-rep machine work to manage fatigue.
muscles.training_notes: Squat to depth for loaded stretch; leg extensions isolate and train the rectus femoris best when the hip is extended. Deep-range work is high-yield.

muscles.name: Posterior Deltoid (Rear Delt)

landmarks.notes: Commonly undertrained; gets partial indirect work from horizontal rowing. Tolerates high direct volume. Estimate only.

muscles.frequency_notes: ~2-3x/week; pairs naturally with back and side-delt work.
muscles.training_notes: Reverse pec-deck, cable rear-delt flyes, and wide-elbow rows. Keep loads light and reps higher; effort near failure matters more than heavy weight.

muscles.name: Lateral Deltoid (Side Delt)

landmarks.notes: Receives little effective indirect work, tolerates high direct volume, and is a common priority for width. The 24-26 MRV is a model-based upper-bound estimate, not a directly measured ceiling — high-volume dose-response data are sparse. The cited Enes 2024 set-progression trial is on the lower limb (quadriceps), not this muscle, and even there found no significant hypertrophy difference between constant and progressively higher-volume training (only a possible small benefit at higher volumes, held with low certainty). Treat this ceiling as uncertain and individual.

muscles.frequency_notes: Responds well to high frequency (2-4x/week) of lateral raise variations.
muscles.training_notes: Lateral raises (dumbbell and cable) are the staple. The top of the raise adds little tension; cables/lean-away variations load the lengthened position better.

muscles.name: Spinal Erectors (Erector Spinae)

landmarks.notes: Receives heavy indirect loading from squats, deadlifts, rows, and carries, so dedicated direct volume is usually low. Estimate only.

muscles.frequency_notes: Often sufficiently trained by compound lifts; add direct extension work if lagging.
muscles.training_notes: Deadlift variations and back extensions are the primary direct stimulus. Manage fatigue: the lumbar erectors are involved in many lifts.

muscles.name: Triceps Brachii

landmarks.notes: Receives substantial indirect work from all pressing; the long head especially responds to overhead (lengthened) training. Estimate only.

muscles.frequency_notes: ~2x/week direct, on top of pressing involvement.
muscles.training_notes: Include an overhead extension to load the long head at length (see maeo-2023-triceps-overhead), plus a pushdown for the lateral/medial heads.

muscles.name: Upper Back (Trapezius & Rhomboids)

landmarks.notes: Tolerates high volume and frequency; receives substantial indirect work from rows, deadlifts, and carries. The 24-26 MRV is a model-based upper-bound estimate, not a directly measured ceiling — high-volume dose-response data are sparse. The cited Enes 2024 set-progression trial is on the lower limb (quadriceps), not this muscle, and even there found no significant hypertrophy difference between constant and progressively higher-volume training (only a possible small benefit at higher volumes, held with low certainty). Treat this ceiling as uncertain and individual.

muscles.frequency_notes: ~2-3x/week; overlaps heavily with lat and rear-delt training.
muscles.training_notes: Rows train the mid-traps/rhomboids; add shrugs or upright variations for upper traps if prioritized.

contraindications.$comment: Practice-based movement-screening heuristics (Grade D) mapping a reported injury region to movement_patterns the plan engine should avoid. exclude_patterns are avoided at any severity; caution_patterns are additionally avoided at moderate/severe. Not medical advice — see content/05-recovery/injury-management.

lower-back.note: Loaded spinal flexion/compression can aggravate low-back injury; prefer machine/supported leg and back work.

knee.note: Loaded knee flexion (squats, lunges) and full-range knee extension are the classic patellofemoral/knee aggravators. At mild you keep everything (just train in a pain-free range and prefer machine/controlled ranges); at moderate/severe these are pulled and direct quad work is minimised in favour of hamstring, hip and calf work while the knee settles.

shoulder.note: Overhead pressing and the lateral-raise abduction arc are the classic irritated-shoulder aggravators (impingement / painful arc). Overhead pressing is avoided at any severity; at moderate/severe, hard horizontal pressing and lateral raises are pulled too — prefer neutral-grip machine work and pulls in a pain-free range.

elbow.note: Direct arm isolation can aggravate elbow tendinopathy; reduce volume and prefer neutral grips.

wrist.note: Loaded wrist flexion/extension; avoid direct wrist work while symptomatic.

hip.note: Deep loaded hip flexion; prefer controlled ranges and machine support.

neck.note: Avoid direct neck loading while symptomatic.

ankle.note: Loaded plantarflexion; reduce calf work while symptomatic.

guidelines.name: Cardio alongside hypertrophy training
guidelines.summary: Cardio and lifting are compatible. At the whole-muscle level the cost is about zero; at the fibre level it is small and concentrated in running. The practical levers are modality, weekly dose, and how much recovery is left over. Dose ranges below are practical models, not measured constants.

modalities.name: Walking and incline walking
modalities.note: No measured cost to muscle size. The main way to raise expenditure without spending recovery, which is why steps come before structured cardio in a deficit.

modalities.name: Cycling
modalities.note: No fibre-size interference in the fibre-level meta-analysis. One caveat: in the HIIT-specific meta it was cycling, not running, that trended toward blunting lower-body strength.

modalities.name: Rowing, elliptical, ski erg
modalities.note: No direct concurrent-training evidence. Grouped with cycling because they share the low eccentric loading that is the presumed mechanism.

modalities.name: Running
modalities.note: The one modality with a measured fibre-level cost: type I fibre hypertrophy was reduced when the aerobic work was running (SMD -0.81), and not when it was cycling. Higher eccentric loading and muscle damage are the presumed mechanism.

modalities.name: High-intensity intervals
modalities.note: Did not compromise hypertrophy or upper-body strength, but did cost a little lower-body strength (ES -0.248). Intervals also cost more recovery per minute than steady work.

hypertrophy.note: The health floor, not a fat-loss dose. Steps carry most of the health return; the sessions add cardiorespiratory fitness at a dose low enough that the interference gradient stays flat. Do not drop to zero in a gaining phase.

strength.note: Same floor as hypertrophy, with more care around same-session work: explosive and maximal strength are the outcomes that show interference first.

fat-loss.note: Diet does the heavy lifting. Steps come first because they cost almost no recovery and defend the expenditure that falls on its own during a deficit; structured cardio is the third lever, after food and steps.

recomposition.note: Between the two. Keep lifting volume and protein fixed and let steps absorb most of the expenditure work.

timing_rules.rule: Keep hard lower-body cardio off the day of, and the day before, a leg session.
timing_rules.note: The clearest case of cardio and lifting competing for the same muscles rather than the same day.

timing_rules.rule: If cardio and lifting share a session, lift first.
timing_rules.note: Commonly recommended and cheap to follow, but the fibre-level meta-analysis found no difference by same-session training order. Treat it as a hedge, not an evidenced rule.

timing_rules.rule: When cardio and lifting share a day, separate them by about six hours where practical.
timing_rules.note: Extrapolated from acute fatigue timelines, not from a concurrent-training trial that tested separation.

indicators.hindering: Legs go flat or slide while upper-body lifts keep climbing.

indicators.signal: Weekly hard sets against your volume landmarks
indicators.helping: When a lift stalls, it stalls at or above MRV, which is a lifting-volume problem.
indicators.hindering: A muscle stalls while its weekly sets sit inside the productive MEV-MAV range, which points outside the gym.

indicators.helping: Weight tracks the direction your goal needs.
indicators.hindering: Weight drifts down while you are trying to gain, or falls faster than about 1 percent of bodyweight per week.

indicators.helping: Energy, sleep and motivation hold steady or rise across a block.
indicators.hindering: The block average drifts low and stays there.

indicators.signal: Reps held across sets at the same load
indicators.helping: You hold your reps set to set, or need less rest for the same reps.
indicators.hindering: Reps fall off sharply from the first set to the last at loads you used to handle.

indicators.helping: The same weights feel the same or easier.
indicators.hindering: The same weights feel harder week over week.

indicators.helping: Trending down, the expected sign of improving cardiovascular fitness.
indicators.hindering: Trending up alongside the other signals, a common marker of accumulated fatigue.

indicators.signal: Appetite, sleep, and whether you want to train
indicators.helping: You eat and sleep well and still look forward to sessions.
indicators.hindering: Appetite is suppressed, sleep is broken, or training feels like a chore it did not used to feel like.

guidelines.scale_back_protocol: Halve your structured cardio for two to three weeks and hold everything else constant: same lifting volume, same calories, same sleep. If the stalled lifts start moving, cardio load was the limiter. Change one thing at a time or the test tells you nothing.
